newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Chances slim of deal on cuts in car pollution.
newsitem.headline: Chances slim of deal on cuts in car pollution.

text.p: European Union environment ministers could fail next month to resolve their differences over draft European Union rules on vehicle engine emissions and fuel quality, designed to cut air pollution by the year 2010.

The EU states are deeply divided over European Commission proposals to introduce in the year 2000 stricter limits on the amount of sulphur, benzene, aromatics and cetane allowed in motor fuels, senior Commission energy official Johannes Maters told a conference on Wednesday on refining, vehicle technology and fuel quality.

Governments are also split over the precise timing of a ban on leaded petrol, which the Commission wants to bring in by 2000, and disagree over the need to set even stricter emission reduction targets for the year 2005, Maters said.

Southern countries like Spain and Portugal, whose refineries import highly sulphurous crude oil from the Gulf, would have great difficulty meeting the Commission's target of cutting the maximum sulphur content in diesel from 500 to 350 parts per million (ppm) in 2000, another EU official told Reuters.

And their refining industries had threatened to move operations out of the EU altogether if European governments imposed too stringent fuel quality standards, the official, who declined to be identified, said.
By contrast, several of the northern EU states, including Germany, were pressing for even tighter limits on pollutants, Maters said.
He predicted the Dutch, who hold the EU presidency, would have difficulty achieving their goal of brokering a compromise at the June 19-20 environment ministers meeting in Brussels.

Even if a provisional deal is reached at June's Environment Council, there will be an arduous round of negotiations with the European Parliament before the draft directive COM(96)248 makes it onto the statute books, Maters warned.

On April 10 the parliament adopted dozens of amendments tightening the fuel norms and engine standards put forward by the Commission, criticising the EU executive for having failed to consult more widely than the car and oil industries in drawing up its plans.

Maters, himself a Dutchman and a former employee of the Anglo-Dutch oil company Shell, said he did not agree with the parliament that the new emission standards should be based on the best available technology.

The Commission had worked closely with the oil and motor industries to draft standards that were cost-effective and took into account the strategic, economic and job-providing importance of these sectors, he explained.

The EU's refining sector was facing decreasing profit margins and increasingly tough environmental protection requirements. It needed a minimum level of profit to make the necessary investments in pollution reduction.

Representatives at the conference of the EU oil industry went further and openly attacked the parliament's demands, which include for petrol cutting the benzene level to one percent and the sulphur content to 30 ppm.
The Commission has proposed limits of two percent and 200 ppm respectively for these substances, which both produce air-borne pollutants that damage human health.
Texaco's strategy adviser Mats Fredriksson said the parliament's demands would produce "minor improvements, while the cost escalates five- or six-fold".

He said new reformulated motor fuels of the type used in Finland were not an answer to Europe's pollution problems since they did nothing to reduce nitrogen oxide emissions, a claim refuted by Arco Chemical Europe, which pioneers the product.
Arco's director of government relations Jonathan Kapstein told Reuters the limits proposed by the parliament were "very strict but...perfectly achievable on the fuel side".
Europe's oil companies were "rich beyond the dreams of avarice" and could afford the investments Euro-MPs wanted.
The parliament's demands also won a degree of support from the European vehicle manufacturers association (ACEA).

Anders Roej from Volvo's fuels technology department submitted a paper to the conference pointing out that ACEA's fuel charter, agreed in 1994, mirrors the parliament's demands on sulphur and benzene limits.
Whatever the future of the Commission's planned emission reduction targets for 2000, Energy Commissioner Christos Papoutsis has pledged to consider new, tighter rules for 2005.
While EU officials worked closely with the oil and car industry in drawing up the current draft rules, getting industry support for tougher standards may prove more difficult.
"Europe's problems can be solved by the Commission's (current) proposal," said Texaco's Fredriksson.
He said any future attempts to introduce higher air quality standards should target pollution from source other than the transport sector, such as power stations.
